title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 5
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: Cognitive Effects of Bilingualism
passages.text:
For much of the twentieth century, bilingualism was viewed with suspicion in Western educational contexts, often regarded as a cognitive burden that confused the developing mind and impeded academic progress. Monolingual instruction policies were justified by the assumption that exposure to two languages simultaneously created interference and mental overload. This perspective, though once nearly universal among educators and psychologists, has been thoroughly overturned by contemporary cognitive science research demonstrating that bilingual experience confers distinct cognitive advantages unavailable to monolingual speakers.

Recent neurolinguistic studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) reveal that bilingual brains exhibit fundamentally different patterns of neural activation compared to monolingual brains. When bilinguals process either language, they activate not just the regions specialized for that particular language but also suppress activation in the other language system—a process requiring inhibitory control that strengthens the brain's executive function networks. Executive functions encompass working memory, cognitive flexibility, and selective attention—higher-order cognitive capacities that correlate strongly with academic achievement, problem-solving ability, and behavioral self-regulation. This continual mental exercise of managing two language systems appears to enhance these capacities even in non-linguistic domains.

Longitudinal studies following bilingual children through school years document measurable advantages in cognitive flexibility, the ability to switch between different mental frameworks or problem-solving strategies. When faced with tasks requiring perspective-taking or mental set shifting—such as solving novel mathematical problems or understanding another person's viewpoint—bilingual children consistently outperform age-matched monolingual controls. Furthermore, the bilingual advantage extends to convergent and divergent thinking, with bilingual children demonstrating superior creative problem-solving and the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems.

Compellingly, research suggests that these cognitive benefits accumulate across the lifespan. Epidemiological studies tracking cognitively normal older adults over extended periods found that bilingualism delays the onset of cognitive decline and dementia by approximately four to five years—a protective effect comparable to or exceeding that of higher education, exercising regularly, or maintaining social engagement. The proposed mechanism involves the constant cognitive stimulation of managing multiple language systems, maintaining a cognitive reserve that slows neurodegeneration when age-related brain changes occur.

However, the bilingual advantage is not universally automatic; it depends critically on individual and environmental factors. The degree of proficiency in each language matters significantly: individuals with balanced bilingualism—near-native proficiency in both languages—show stronger cognitive advantages than those with asymmetrical proficiency. Additionally, the social context of bilingualism influences outcomes: children who view their bilingualism as an asset and receive supportive educational environments show enhanced benefits, whereas those experiencing stigmatization of their non-dominant language may show diminished advantages or even cognitive costs from interrupted language development.

passages.title: Ancient Egyptian Irrigation Systems
passages.text:
Ancient Egyptian civilization was fundamentally shaped by the Nile River, which provided water, fertile soil, and transportation routes essential for sustaining a complex society across an otherwise arid landscape. Yet the Nile's contribution to Egyptian prosperity extended far beyond its annual flooding cycle; it was the deliberate engineering of water management systems that transformed flood waters into a controlled resource capable of supporting a population exceeding several million in antiquity. The sophistication of Egyptian irrigation technology, developed and refined over nearly three thousand years, stands as testament to the engineering ingenuity of one of history's earliest hydraulic civilizations.

The foundation of Egyptian hydraulic engineering was the nilometer, a structure designed to measure the annual flood's height and predict the expected inundation extent. Nilometers consisted of a vertical well connected by channels to the river, with measurement scales carved into interior walls, allowing hydraulic officials to calculate the expected flood volume and plan resource allocation accordingly. This systematic monitoring transformed what might have been an unpredictable natural phenomenon into a managed resource. The preserved nilometer at Aswan, still intact after millennia, demonstrates the precision and durability of Egyptian construction. By measuring flood heights year by year, Egyptian administrators could anticipate abundant harvests when floods reached optimal levels or prepare for potential famine when floods fell below critical thresholds.

Beyond measurement, Egyptians engineered an extensive network of irrigation basins and canals that captured and redistributed floodwaters. Basin irrigation systems, consisting of terraced earthen reservoirs, stored water at the height of inundation. As the river receded in subsequent seasons, water from these basins could be released through a system of canals to irrigate fields throughout the growing season. Dikes constructed between basins, sometimes reaching lengths of several kilometers, regulated water flow with remarkable precision. Archaeological evidence suggests that these systems evolved significantly over time: the Old Kingdom saw relatively simple, localized basin systems, while the New Kingdom boasted integrated regional networks capable of moving water dozens of kilometers from the river.

The mechanical innovations supporting Egyptian irrigation deserved particular attention. The shaduf, a hand-operated lever mechanism consisting of a weighted pole with an attached bucket, emerged during the New Kingdom and dramatically extended irrigation reach by allowing workers to lift water to higher-elevation fields. Rather than depending solely on gravity-fed systems constrained by terrain, the shaduf enabled irrigation in regions not naturally served by canal systems. Alongside the shaduf, Egyptians developed the screw pump—an Archimedean screw—which further expanded the altitude at which water could be delivered. These devices represented pragmatic mechanical innovations addressing specific engineering challenges rather than theoretical advancement, yet their contribution to expanding arable land and supporting population growth proved transformative.

The legacy of Egyptian irrigation extends beyond ancient Egypt itself. The hydraulic expertise developed along the Nile influenced irrigation practices throughout the Mediterranean and Near East. Roman engineers, who conquered Egypt and inherited its hydraulic traditions, incorporated Egyptian canal-and-basin principles into their own aqueduct systems. The fundamental insight animating Egyptian hydraulic engineering—that water is a manageable resource to be measured, stored, and strategically distributed—became a cornerstone of settled civilization, enabling societies throughout history to overcome environmental constraints and support growing populations.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the predominant view of bilingualism among twentieth-century Western educators?
questions.correctAnswer: It created confusion and impeded academic progress
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states bilingualism 'was viewed with suspicion' and 'was justified by the assumption that exposure to two languages simultaneously created interference and mental overload.'
options: It enhanced cognitive flexibility
It created confusion and impeded academic progress
It had no effect on academic achievement
It was equally beneficial as monolingualism

questions.prompt: The word 'inhibitory' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: suppressing or restraining
questions.explanation: Inhibitory control means the ability to suppress or restrain one language system while activating the other.
options: preventing all language development
suppressing or restraining
describing language structure
slowing cognitive growth

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what three components comprise executive functions?
questions.correctAnswer: Working memory, cognitive flexibility, and selective attention
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines executive functions as 'working memory, cognitive flexibility, and selective attention.'
options: Language production, comprehension, and pronunciation
Reading, writing, and speaking skills
Working memory, cognitive flexibility, and selective attention
Mathematical reasoning, logic, and analysis

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the passage about the relationship between bilingualism and problem-solving ability?
questions.correctAnswer: Bilingual experience strengthens the cognitive skills required for effective problem-solving
questions.explanation: The passage explains that executive functions enhanced by bilingualism correlate with problem-solving ability, and bilingual children show superior creative problem-solving.
options: Monolingual individuals are better problem-solvers
Bilingual experience strengthens the cognitive skills required for effective problem-solving
Problem-solving ability is unaffected by language exposure
Only native bilinguals can solve complex problems

questions.prompt: Why does the author cite epidemiological studies of older adults in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To demonstrate that bilingual advantages extend throughout the entire lifespan
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 presents these studies as evidence that 'cognitive benefits accumulate across the lifespan,' showing long-term protective effects.
options: To argue that young people should not be bilingual
To demonstrate that bilingual advantages extend throughout the entire lifespan
To show that aging eliminates bilingual cognitive benefits
To prove that monolingualism is healthier in old age

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a factor affecting the degree of bilingual cognitive advantage?
questions.correctAnswer: The alphabetical order of the two languages
questions.explanation: The passage mentions proficiency level, social context, and language balance, but not alphabetical order of languages.
options: The degree of proficiency in each language
The social context and cultural attitudes toward bilingualism
The balance between proficiency in both languages
The alphabetical order of the two languages

questions.prompt: According to the passage, by how many years does bilingualism delay the onset of cognitive decline?
questions.correctAnswer: By approximately four to five years
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states bilingualism 'delays the onset of cognitive decline and dementia by approximately four to five years.'
options: By one to two years
By approximately four to five years
By ten or more years
The passage does not specify a duration

questions.prompt: The word 'convergent' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: focused toward a single solution
questions.explanation: Convergent thinking contrasts with divergent thinking; it focuses on finding one correct solution rather than generating multiple possibilities.
options: beginning or starting point
focused toward a single solution
scattered or disconnected
imaginative and creative

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential meaning of: 'When bilinguals process either language, they activate not just the regions specialized for that particular language but also suppress activation in the other language system.'
questions.correctAnswer: Processing one language requires both activating and suppressing different brain regions
questions.explanation: The sentence describes the neurological process of managing two language systems simultaneously through both activation and inhibition.
options: Bilinguals cannot activate both languages at once
Processing one language requires both activating and suppressing different brain regions
Monolinguals use more brain regions than bilinguals
Only specialized language regions contribute to bilingual speech

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.correctAnswer: A,C,E
questions.explanation: These capture the core arguments: the reversal of historical negative views (A), neurological evidence for cognitive advantages (C), and the importance of context and proficiency (E).
options: A. Twentieth-century views of bilingualism as harmful have been overturned by modern neuroscience research.
B. All bilingual people automatically become mathematicians.
C. Bilingual experience strengthens executive function networks through active management of two language systems.
D. Monolingual brains are more efficient than bilingual brains.
E. The cognitive benefits of bilingualism depend on proficiency levels and supportive social contexts.
F. Bilingualism only provides advantages to young children.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the primary purpose of the nilometer in ancient Egypt?
questions.correctAnswer: To measure the Nile's annual flood height and predict inundation extent
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states the nilometer was 'designed to measure the annual flood's height and predict the expected inundation extent.'
options: To prevent flooding from damaging crops
To measure the Nile's annual flood height and predict inundation extent
To generate power for grinding grain
To defend Egyptian cities from invaders

questions.prompt: The word 'inundation' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: flooding or submersion under water
questions.explanation: Inundation refers to the submersion of land under water, in this context the Nile's annual flooding.
options: a dry period with no rain
flooding or submersion under water
the flow of water downstream
underground water sources

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the primary function of basin irrigation systems in ancient Egypt?
questions.correctAnswer: To store floodwaters and release them gradually throughout the growing season
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes basins as 'terraced earthen reservoirs' that 'stored water at the height of inundation' and could 'be released through a system of canals.'
options: To prevent flooding by channeling water away from settlements
To store floodwaters and release them gradually throughout the growing season
To collect drinking water for the population
To power mechanical devices through flowing water

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the passage about the difference between Old Kingdom and New Kingdom irrigation systems?
questions.correctAnswer: New Kingdom systems were more extensive and integrated than earlier systems
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states Old Kingdom saw 'relatively simple, localized basin systems, while the New Kingdom boasted integrated regional networks capable of moving water dozens of kilometers.'
options: Old Kingdom irrigation was more advanced than New Kingdom systems
New Kingdom systems were more extensive and integrated than earlier systems
Both periods used identical irrigation techniques
Irrigation was not used during either period

questions.prompt: Why does the author discuss the shaduf in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate how mechanical innovations extended irrigation capabilities to higher elevations
questions.explanation: The shaduf is presented as a specific example of mechanical innovation that 'dramatically extended irrigation reach by allowing workers to lift water to higher-elevation fields.'
options: To show that Egyptians invented all modern technology
To illustrate how mechanical innovations extended irrigation capabilities to higher elevations
To argue that gravity-fed systems were superior to mechanical ones
To prove that Archimedean screws existed before the shaduf

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a component of Egyptian irrigation technology?
questions.correctAnswer: Underground aqueducts built from stone
questions.explanation: The passage mentions nilometers, basins, canals, dikes, shadufs, and screw pumps, but not underground stone aqueducts.
options: Nilometers for measuring flood heights
Basin and canal systems for water distribution
Underground aqueducts built from stone
The shaduf mechanical lifting device

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what specific advantage did the shaduf provide over simple gravity-fed canal systems?
questions.correctAnswer: It allowed water to be lifted to higher-elevation fields
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the shaduf 'dramatically extended irrigation reach by allowing workers to lift water to higher-elevation fields,' overcoming terrain constraints.
options: It required less skilled labor to operate
It allowed water to be lifted to higher-elevation fields
It was the first irrigation device ever invented
It prevented flooding by blocking water flow

questions.prompt: The word 'pragmatic' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: practical and problem-focused
questions.explanation: Pragmatic means concerned with practical results rather than theory; the passage notes these were 'pragmatic mechanical innovations addressing specific engineering challenges.'
options: theoretical and abstract
practical and problem-focused
expensive and inefficient
ancient and outdated

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential meaning of: 'Rather than depending solely on gravity-fed systems constrained by terrain, the shaduf enabled irrigation in regions not naturally served by canal systems.'
questions.correctAnswer: The shaduf overcame geographical limitations of gravity-fed irrigation methods
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts the limitations of gravity-fed systems with the shaduf's ability to function regardless of terrain constraints.
options: Gravity-fed systems were always superior to mechanical lifting
The shaduf overcame geographical limitations of gravity-fed irrigation methods
Canal systems could not function in any terrain
All irrigation systems depend entirely on gravity

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.correctAnswer: A,B,D
questions.explanation: These capture the main themes: the foundational role of the Nile (A), the development of systematic measurement and water storage (B), and the influence on later civilizations (D).
options: A. Ancient Egyptian civilization depended on engineering systems that transformed the unpredictable Nile into a controlled water resource.
B. Nilometers, basin systems, and canals allowed Egyptians to manage seasonal flooding systematically.
C. Modern irrigation systems are completely unrelated to ancient Egyptian innovations.
D. Egyptian hydraulic expertise influenced irrigation practices throughout the Mediterranean and Near East.
E. The shaduf was the only irrigation device ever used in ancient Egypt.
F. Romans destroyed all Egyptian irrigation infrastructure.
